California "Attorney With An Attitude" Critiques Prop 215:
"It Is Time To Write A New Law And Pass It As A New Proposition."
Special To Marijuananews

SPECIAL TO MARIJUANANEWS, BY JOAN STEVENS

As various factions stake out positions on the Lockyer/Vasconcellos guidelines for implementing Proposition 215, some commentators are beginning to publicly say that 215 may be fatally flawed and that a new, improved medical pot law needs to be placed on the ballot in the year 2000.

According to Dale Rasmussen, a Northern California attorney who specializes in Prop. 215 defense and other marijuana cases, "the people who wrote 215 were well-intentioned, but the law fails to take into account so many things, and it is obviously not working the way its proponents and medical marijuana users believed it would."
See

Rasmussen isn’t just an armchair quarterback. As a litigator who describes himself as "an attorney with an attitude," Rasmussen has won high-profile, potentially precedent-setting cases in rural Butte County, a venue that is considerably more hostile to marijuana defendants than in most other parts of California.

Rasmussen helped medical pot and hemp activist David Kasakove beat pot possession charges, and then utilized Kasakove’s case as a wedge to force courts to rule on whether police should be forced to return marijuana to innocent defendants whose charges have been dismissed.

"We haven’t been successful in getting his pot back so far," Rasmussen admits, "but it’s important that we keep trying and here’s why: until appellate courts rule on this in a circulated, published opinion, the return of seized marijuana will continue to be handled on a case by case basis, with none of the cases setting a statewide precedent."

Rasmussen said Kasakove’s case is headed for the State Supreme Court.

"One of the main problems of 215 is that it did not address enough issues," he explained. "It doesn’t prohibit police from seizing medicine. It doesn’t prohibit police from using a sighting of medical marijuana as justification for a search warrant, where they kick in your door with approval from a judge. It doesn’t force police to give medicine back. It doesn’t explicitly challenge the idea that marijuana is contraband. It doesn’t require that police reimburse you for out-of-pocket costs or other costs associated with a medical marijuana arrest."

Echoing concerns of other observers who note that marijuana arrests seem to have increased because people believe 215 gives them immunity from arrest or prosecution if they have a medical recommendation to use pot, Rasmussen notes that "courts have ruled that this is only an affirmative defense that can be used at trial."

"People are still being arrested, jailed, and then they have to post bail and find an attorney and go through months of hearings and motions," he said. "They may eventually be found innocent by virtue of their doctor’s recommendation, but they go through hell in the meantime."

Rasmussen has seen other problems as well.

"The law stipulates oral or written recommendations, but you can’t submit that is ironclad evidence because it’s defined as ‘hearsay.’ You can’t even submit the written recommendation byb itself- in some cases we’ve had to subpoena the doctors, at great expense to the defendant and the doctor. And the law doesn’t address how medical marijuana defenses affect other legal issues. For example, in child custody, divorce cases, forfeiture and other civil actions, the use of medical marijuana is considered a negative, a disqualifier, something that can be used against you. And if you’re on probation or out on bail, you are prohibited from using controlled substances, whether it’s medical marijuana or not. There are too many loopholes," he said.

Saying he is an attorney and not an activist or a political advisor, Rasmussen refused to speculate on what would happen if an expanded version of 215, or a replacement ballot initiative, were to be offered to voters.

"Personally, I think you could pass a strongly-worded medical marijuana law, but regardless of whatever implementation policies are put into effect, 215 is a poorly written law that guarantees virtually no rights," he insists. "It is time to write a new law and pass it as a new proposition."

Rasmussen says he is spending much of his time litigating Prop. 215 issues and studying statewide 215 decisions.

"I have plenty of ideas about how to craft a medical pot law that works. I’m willing to write a new medical marijuana ballot proposition that incorporates everything that needs to be there in a comprehensive and solid manner that’ll stand up in courts," he said. "People can call me at 530-342-5130 if they want to talk about doing that."
